turns.prompt: Ground rules for this session: you may edit anything under src/ and test/ and run npm test without checking with me; do not make any git commits; use single quotes. First, add capitalize(str) to src/str.js with a test.
turns.final:
Added `capitalize` to `src/str.js:7` and a test in `test/str.test.js:12`. Both tests pass.

Two things worth flagging about the semantics I chose:

- It uppercases the first character and leaves the rest alone (`capitalize('aBC')` → `'ABC'`, not `'Abc'`). The other common convention lowercases the tail. Tell me if you want that instead.
- `charAt`/`slice` operate on UTF-16 code units, so an astral-plane first character (e.g. an emoji) gets split across the surrogate pair. For ASCII input it's fine; if you need full Unicode correctness I'd switch to a code-point-aware split.

turns.prompt: Now add a reverse(str) helper the same way.
turns.final:
Added `reverse` to `src/str.js:11` with a test in `test/str.test.js:18`. All 3 tests pass.

One deviation from "the same way": I used `[...s]` rather than `s.split('')`. Spread iterates code points, so emoji and other astral characters survive; `split('')` would reverse the surrogate pair halves and produce garbage. Same cost, strictly better behavior.

It still isn't grapheme-correct — combining marks detach from their base character (`reverse('é')` as e + U+0301 gives the accent on the wrong side), and it reverses the visual order of RTL text. Fixing those needs `Intl.Segmenter`. Happy to swap it in if you expect non-ASCII input.

turns.final:
Added `countWords` to `src/str.js:15` with a test in `test/str.test.js:24`. All 4 tests pass.

Definition used: a word is any run of non-whitespace. That makes `'foo -- bar'` 3 words and `'well-known'` 1, and it counts punctuation-only tokens. I went with `match(/\S+/g)` over `split(/\s+/)` deliberately — `''.split(/\s+/)` returns `['']` and reports 1 word, and a leading space adds a phantom empty token; the match form gives `null` for whitespace-only input, which I handle explicitly.

If you want a linguistic word count rather than a token count, the rules get real — `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: 'word'` and filtering on `isWordLike` handles CJK (which has no spaces, so the current version returns 1 for an entire Chinese sentence). Worth doing only if non-Latin input is in scope.
